title: Windows With Exactly K Kinds
statement:
You get an array of integers nums and a number k. Count the contiguous, non-empty slices of nums that contain exactly k different values.

Slices are counted by position, so equal-looking slices at different places count separately.

examples.why: [1, 2], [1, 2, 1], [2, 1], [1, 3] and [3, 2]. A slice like [2, 1, 3] has three kinds and does not count.
Every slice qualifies: three of length 1, two of length 2, one of length 3. A window that only records its longest valid form at each end would count 3.
The slice must contain the 7 and both 5 and 6: it ends at the 7 and starts at index 0, 1 or 2.

hints: A plain sliding window can count slices with at most k kinds easily. Why is 'exactly k' harder for a single window?
Slices with exactly k kinds = slices with at most k kinds − slices with at most k − 1 kinds.

For at-most-k: move the right end one step at a time, add the value to a count map, shrink from the left while the map has more than k keys. Every slice ending at right and starting in [left, right] is valid, so add right − left + 1.

explain.intuition:
A sliding window works when the condition is monotonic: if a slice is valid, every slice inside it is valid too. "At most k kinds" has that property, "exactly k" does not, since a shorter slice may drop to k − 1 kinds. So one window cannot decide where its valid starts end.

The fix is to count something easier twice. For "at most k", fix the right end; the leftmost valid start is found by shrinking, and every start from there to the right end also works. So each step adds right − left + 1 slices. Slices with exactly k kinds are those with at most k, minus those with at most k − 1. Two linear passes, no nested loops.
steps: Write atMost(m): a window with a count map and left = 0, total = 0.
For each right, add nums[right] to the map. While the map has more than m keys, remove nums[left] (deleting keys that reach 0) and move left right.
Add right − left + 1 to total: all slices ending at right that start at or after left.
pitfalls: Counting one slice per window position instead of right − left + 1. That counts only the longest valid slice at each end, like 3 instead of 6 for [4, 4, 4].
Keeping keys with count 0 in the map, so the number of kinds never shrinks.
Trying to shrink the window as soon as it has exactly k kinds. Valid slices with a shorter start are then lost, as with [2, 1, 2, 1, 2].

solutions.title: Every start, growing set
solutions.idea: Fix the start, extend the end and keep a set of seen values. Count while the set has exactly k values; stop once it has more.

solutions.title: At most k minus at most k − 1
solutions.idea: Counting slices with at most m kinds is a standard window. Exactly k is the difference of two such counts.

followups: Do it in one pass with two left pointers: one for 'at most k' and one for 'at most k − 1'.
Count slices whose sum is exactly a target, with all values non-negative. Does the same subtraction trick apply?
